content: Candidal Osteomyelitis The preferred treatment for candidal osteomyelitis involves administering fluconazole at a dose of 400 mg (6 mg/kg) either intravenously or orally once daily. Alternatively, lipid-based amphotericin B can be given at a dose of 3–5 mg/kg daily for two weeks, followed by fluconazole. For patients who cannot tolerate these options, alternative regimens include caspofungin with a 70 mg loading dose followed by 50 mg/day intravenously, micafungin at 100 mg/day intravenously, or anidulafungin with a 200 mg intravenous loading dose followed by 100 mg/day intravenously. Chronic Osteomyelitis The management of chronic osteomyelitis requires systemic antibiotic therapy tailored to culture and susceptibility results. This is combined with surgical debridement to remove infected or necrotic tissue. Osteomyelitis Contiguous with Vascular Insufficiency For osteomyelitis associated with vascular insufficiency, the treatment includes systemic antibiotics based on culture and susceptibility results, surgical debridement, and revascularization procedures if feasible. Osteomyelitis Contiguous without Vascular Insufficiency The preferred regimen for this condition includes vancomycin at 1 g intravenously every 12 hours, combined with either ceftazidime at 2 g intravenously every 8 hours or cefepime at 2 g intravenously every 12 hours. An alternative regimen involves linezolid at 600 mg orally or intravenously twice daily, combined with either ceftazidime or cefepime at the same dosages. For infections caused by gram-negative bacilli, ciprofloxacin at 750 mg orally twice daily or linezolid at 600 mg orally or intravenously twice daily is recommended. For Staphylococcus aureus infections, ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin (750 mg orally once daily if susceptible) can be combined with rifampin (300–450 mg orally twice daily or 600 mg orally once daily if susceptible). Methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) infections can be treated with nafcillin, oxacillin, or cefazolin at appropriate intravenous dosages. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infections require vancomycin at 15–20 mg/kg intravenously every 8–12 hours, targeting trough concentrations of 15–20 mg/L. Diabetic Foot Infections For chronic diabetic foot infections, treatment options include levofloxacin (750 mg intravenously or orally once daily), cefoxitin (1 g intravenously every 4 hours or 2 g intravenously every 6–8 hours), ceftriaxone (1–2 g/day intravenously or intramuscularly every 12–24 hours), ampicillin-sulbactam (1.5–3 g intravenously or intramuscularly every 6 hours), moxifloxacin (400 mg intravenously or orally once daily), ertapenem (1 g intravenously or intramuscularly once daily), tigecycline (100 mg intravenously followed by 50 mg intravenously every 12 hours), or imipenem-cilastatin (0.5–1 g intravenously every 6–8 hours). For patients with recent antibiotic use, the same regimens apply. High-risk MRSA infections can be treated with linezolid (600 mg intravenously or orally every 12 hours), daptomycin (4 mg/kg intravenously once daily), or vancomycin (15–20 mg/kg intravenously every 8–12 hours, targeting trough levels of 10–20 mg/L). For high-risk Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections, piperacillin-tazobactam (3.375 g intravenously every 6–8 hours) is recommended. Polymicrobial infections require a combination of vancomycin, linezolid, or daptomycin with piperacillin-tazobactam, imipenem-cilastatin, ertapenem, or meropenem. Alternatively, metronidazole can be combined with ceftazidime, cefepime, or aztreonam. Foot Bone Infections Preferred treatment includes ciprofloxacin (750 mg orally twice daily) or levofloxacin (750 mg orally once daily). Alternative regimens involve ceftazidime (2 g intravenously every 8 hours), cefepime (2 g intravenously every 8 hours), or meropenem (1 g intravenously every 8 hours). Foot Puncture Wounds Management involves wound cleansing, administration of a tetanus booster if indicated, and obtaining an X-ray to rule out the presence of a radio-opaque foreign body. Hematogenous Osteomyelitis For cases where MRSA is likely, vancomycin (15–20 mg/kg intravenously every 8–12 hours) is combined with ceftriaxone (1–2 g/day intravenously or intramuscularly every 12–24 hours), ceftazidime (2 g intravenously every 8 hours), or cefepime (2 g intravenously every 12 hours). If MRSA is unlikely, nafcillin or oxacillin is combined with one of the aforementioned cephalosporins. Alternative regimens include linezolid (600 mg orally or intravenously twice daily) or daptomycin (4 mg/kg intravenously once daily) as substitutes for vancomycin, and ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, or aztreonam as substitutes for third-generation cephalosporins. Hemoglobinopathy-Associated Osteomyelitis Preferred treatment includes ciprofloxacin (400 mg intravenously every 12 hours) or ceftriaxone (2 g intravenously every 24 hours). Alternatively, ciprofloxacin (750 mg orally twice daily) or levofloxacin (750 mg orally once daily) can be administered for six weeks. Prosthetic Joint Infections For MSSA/MSSE infections, nafcillin or oxacillin (2 g intravenously every 4 hours) plus rifampin (300 mg orally twice daily) or cefazolin (2 g intravenously every 8 hours) plus rifampin is recommended for 2–6 weeks, followed by ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin plus rifampin for 3–6 months. For MRSA/MRSE infections, vancomycin (15–20 mg/kg intravenously every 8–12 hours) plus rifampin is used for 2–6 weeks, followed by ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin plus rifampin for 3–6 months. Streptococcal infections are treated with penicillin G or ceftriaxone for 4–6 weeks. Enterococcal infections require ampicillin or penicillin G for penicillin-susceptible strains, and vancomycin for penicillin-resistant strains. Propionibacterium acnes infections are treated with penicillin G or ceftriaxone for 4–6 weeks. Gram-negative enteric bacilli infections are managed with ertapenem, ceftriaxone, or cefepime for 4–6 weeks. Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections require cefepime or meropenem combined with tobramycin for 4–6 weeks. Spinal Implant Infections Treatment regimens for spinal implant infections mirror those for prosthetic joint infections, with similar antibiotic choices and durations. Sternal Infections Preferred treatment includes vancomycin (15–30 mg/kg intravenously every 8–12 hours, targeting a trough of 15–20 μg/mL) or nafcillin (2 g intravenously every 4 hours). Linezolid (600 mg intravenously or orally twice daily) is an alternative option.
